33.0.s.en: 1. In God's name he invites Job to dialogue with him

33.0.0.en: 1 "Wherefore, Job, I pray thee, hear my speeches, and hearken to all my words. 2 Behold, now I have opened my mouth, my tongue hath spoken in my mouth. 3 My words shall be of the uprightness of my heart: and my lips shall utter knowledge clearly. 4 The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life. 5 If thou canst answer me, set thy words in order before me, stand up. 6 Behold, I am according to thy wish in God's stead: I also am formed out of the clay. 7 Behold, my terror shall not make thee afraid, neither shall my hand be heavy upon thee.

33.0.1.en: Wherefore, Job, I pray thee, hear my speeches, and hearken to all my words [1].

33.0.2.en: None of the elders dared to address Job, mentioning his name, but this young man, despite the difference in age, says: [Hear now, O Job, my speeches, and hearken to my words] (Job 33:1). There is a difference in age, but both are creatures, and it is fitting for each of them to listen to the other.

33.0.3.en: If it is fitting for the young in age to obey their elders, then everyone must listen to one another. So we need not wonder that the young Elihu begins his speech to the godly old man Job saying: [Hear now, O Job, my speeches, and hearken to my words] (Job 33:1). He also says with courage and courtesy: "Behold, in this thou art not just" (Job 33:12). He repeats again: [Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I will speak... for I desire to justify thee] (Job 33:31-32).

33.0.4.en: A wonderful picture on both sides: the godly old man of God listens to a young man, with no arrogance on his part and no disdain for his youth. And on the part of the young man, though he converses with the old man frankly, with an open heart and courage, he was extremely courteous and gentle. He wants to justify one who is of his father's age!

33.0.5.en: As Elihu presents his plea to Job, he asks him to listen to him as a sincere friend who loves him, who does not speak to criticize him or terrify him.

33.0.6.en: Elihu quoted some expressions from Job and made clear to him that God is greater than man, and that man has no right to demand an explanation from God for His actions. What Job should realize is that God seeks the salvation of man, not his destruction.

33.0.7.en: Elihu begins by directing his speech to Job, and in the next chapter he directs the speech to Job's friends.

33.0.8.en: This chapter is regarded as an introduction to prepare the hearts of these three friends to listen to him. In this he did not slander Job, but addressed blame to him from the reality of his words in the previous dialogues.

33.0.9.en: He asks him to listen to his words, or his speeches, not only what he addresses to him, but also to [all his words], for he utters divine truth for the benefit of all. He asks him to be long-suffering, to hear the speech to its end, and to keep in mind that what is said is not meant to criticize him and lay blame on him, but for his benefit.

33.0.10.en: Behold, now I have opened my mouth.

33.1.0.en: My tongue hath spoken in my mouth [2].

33.1.1.en: In Barnes's notes on this phrase, Elihu speaks with the words that are in his mouth, uttered by his tongue which moves toward the roof of his palate, because pronunciation in the Hebrew language uses mostly the larynx, the throat and the tongue, whereas in the European languages (Latin and English) it uses mostly the teeth and the lips.

33.1.2.en: He speaks with him from his throat, as one who brings out words carrying a special flavor and a taste full of love. All men speak with their mouths, but few taste their words and examine them first, so that they utter what is good for edification.

33.1.3.en: Elihu was silent throughout the period of the dialogue, interacting inwardly with the dialogue. He did not hasten to criticize or to answer some of the questions, but with wisdom and deliberation he tested the words that were in his mind, so as to utter what is fitting.

33.1.4.en: In a wonderful discourse St. Mar Jacob of Serugh directs us to train ourselves in holy silence and holy speech. Wherever we are occupied with the divine Word, His Holy Spirit leads us to constructive silence as well as constructive speech.

33.1.5.en: * You are the Word who gives a word to those who speak; by You all who speak speak for Your sake.

33.1.6.en: A ray, a radiance and a great light has shone in me, so that I look at You.

33.1.7.en: For by looking at You, the soul is enlightened and acquires goodness.

33.1.8.en: And when the soul departs from You it is filled with darkness, but if it gazes upon You it puts on light, to utter the words of Your news...

33.1.9.en: Silence and speech stand over me and make demands of me.

33.1.10.en: O Lord, order my life according to Your will.

33.1.11.en: If I am silent I marvel, for I feel my insufficiency (for speech). I am silent in wonder, and not in vain arrogance.

33.1.12.en: And if I speak, may my word be according to Your glory and for Your sake.

33.1.13.en: When the soul is filled with silence in wonder at You, this silence is a speech full of all benefit. And when the soul is moved to glorify You with love... it is with love that I move, and I move to glorify You. And in wonder I am silent and do not cease from glorifying You.

33.1.14.en: Grant me, O Lord, wonder (in silence) and the word, and I will be enriched. Every day I marvel, and every day I am moved to speak!

33.2.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh My words shall be of the uprightness of my heart: and my lips shall utter knowledge clearly [3].

33.2.1.en: Elihu says that God, who gave him His Spirit, enables him to speak with a pure heart and to present sincere knowledge, without deceit. It is as though he asks Job to look not at the bare words, but at what is in Elihu's heart of purity toward him, and the uprightness of his aim in the dialogue. His words issue from pure love, without hypocrisy; he speaks in sincerity from his heart, and does not display hollow words. What he utters expresses truthfully what is in his heart.

33.2.2.en: He wanted him not to include him with the three friends, even if the words were similar, because the intentions are entirely different.

33.2.3.en: * He wants to say: It is not out of envy or jealousy that I use this means. Even if the three say the same things as he says, it seems that they did not speak with the same spirit, nor did they do this in defense of God. Judas and the twelve(a) all expressed themselves in the same way concerning the alabaster box of ointment (Jn 12:5-6), but not with the same spirit. Therefore it is fitting for us to examine not the words, but the intention with which each of them expressed himself: how some wanted to crush Job, while the other wanted the opposite.

33.3.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life [4].

33.3.1.en: Many of the Fathers of the Church used this phrase to affirm the divinity of the Holy Spirit as the Creator and Giver of life. If the Father is the Creator and Giver of life, then the three hypostases share together in every divine work. Here he speaks with Job in a spirit of sincere brotherhood, making clear to him that he is the work of the Spirit of God, who gave him life. He is an instrument in the hand of God, who also created Job and gave him life. So Job need not fear dialogue with his fellow in creation and in life, since both owe their existence and life to the Spirit of God. He assures him that both are God's creation, with the same nature, and with its weaknesses that have crept into human nature.

33.3.2.en: * How did (the Book of) Job show clearly that the Spirit is Creator, saying: [The Spirit of God made me]? In a short phrase he showed that He is divine and Creator. If the Spirit is the Creator, then certainly He is not a creature, for the Apostle separates the Creator from the creature, saying: [They worshipped the creature rather than the Creator] (Rom 1:25).

33.3.3.en: St. Ambrose * The Holy Spirit shared with the Son in the work, whether in creation or in resurrection, as Holy Scripture shows: [By the word of the Lord were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth] (Ps 33:6). And also: [The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty teacheth me] (Job 33:4). And also: "Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth" (Ps 104:30).

33.3.4.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * When words of folly are mixed with wise sayings, even wisdom is not kept in the mind, because their folly becomes an object of contempt to the hearer... Here he speaks in fitting order concerning his creation and his receiving of life. He says that he was created by the Spirit, and received life by the breath of God. It is written of Adam at his creation: [He breathed into his face the breath of life; and man became a living soul].

33.3.7.en: Set thy words in order before me.

33.4.1.en: Elihu assures him that if he wishes to enter into dialogue with him, he should know that he has not come as one who rebukes and teaches, but as two equals, made by the Spirit of God. He speaks not to prevail or to dominate, but in a spirit of brotherhood. It is as though he says to him: I am a man like you, and I wish for you what I wish for myself. Receive my words in a spirit of friendliness.

33.4.2.en: Behold, I am according to thy wish in God's stead.

33.5.0.en: I also am formed (molded) out of the clay [6].

33.5.1.en: Umbreit translates it: "I am like you from God"; Noyes: "I am like you, God's creature"; Wemyss: "I am equal to you in the eyes of God"; and Coverdale: "Behold, I am before God as you are; I was formed from the same clay." The Vulgate translation reads: "Behold, God made me as He made you, and from the same clay I was formed." And the Septuagint: "From clay I was formed as you are; we were formed from the same clay."

33.5.2.en: Some hold that the meaning of the phrase in Hebrew is: "I am, according to your mouth, a man of God," that is, I speak in His name as His representative, His ambassador.

33.5.3.en: Since Job was beseeching God to summon him to trial so that he might find his opportunity to defend himself, Elihu came to him asking him to speak with complete frankness as in a court before God.

33.5.4.en: Elihu goes on to reassure Job that though he speaks in the name of the Lord, he is made of frail clay like him, of the dust of the earth. Though God speaks through him, there is nothing in himself to frighten or terrify.

33.5.5.en: * When we are urged to practice some virtue, we must not say that these were partakers of a nature other than ours, or that they were not men. For this reason it was said of the great Elijah: "Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are" (Jas 5:17). Do you see that Elijah showed by his very partaking of sufferings that he was a man like us? Again it was said: [I too am a man subject to the same sufferings as you] (see Wis 7:1). This gives reassurance concerning the sharing of nature.

33.5.6.en: * The nature of Paul the Apostle was no different from our nature; nor was his soul different from our souls, nor did he live in another world, but he dwelt in the same world and was subject to the same laws and customs, yet he surpassed in virtue all men, past and present.

33.5.7.en: Now, where are those who object to the difficulty of virtue and the ease of sin?

33.5.8.en: For this man condemns them by his words: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" (2 Cor 4:17).

33.5.9.en: If his afflictions were bearable and light, how much more so ours, which, compared with his afflictions, become as nothing or mere pleasures?

33.6.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Behold, my terror shall not make thee afraid, neither shall my hand be heavy upon thee [7].

33.6.1.en: With intense longing Job wanted to present his case before God directly, but he felt the awe of God, which made him unable to speak frankly with Him. He says: "Withdraw thine hand far from me: and let not thy dread make me afraid" (Job 13:21), and he says: "Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me" (Job 9:34).

33.6.2.en: Elihu says: {We are equal; there is no fear that will come upon you, and no terror of me that will surprise you, so that you would be unable to take a position of defense with me. My hand will not be heavy upon you, for I am weak like you, and I have no authority over you}.

33.6.3.en: The word "heavy" here is used of a man while he leads an animal that carries loads, and it also indicates a person who is very heavily burdened and so stoops because of the weight of the load.

33.6.4.en: Perhaps because of this meaning Pope Gregory (the Great) felt that Elihu overstepped the bounds of propriety. For while admitting that he bears the same nature as Job, and that he is equal to him, he speaks with surpassing boldness, demanding that Job answer and converse without fear or trembling.

33.7.s.en: 2. His rebuke of Job for using violent expressions

33.7.0.en: 8 "Surely thou hast spoken in mine hearing, and I have heard the voice of thy words, saying, 9 I am clean without transgression, I am innocent; neither is there iniquity in me. 10 Behold, he findeth occasions against me, he counteth me for his enemy, 11 He putteth my feet in the stocks, he marketh all my paths.

33.7.1.en: Surely thou hast spoken in mine hearing, and I have heard the voice of thy words [8].

33.7.2.en: It is clear that Elihu attended all the dialogues, and his ears listened to every word with full attention. Now he begins to comment on what he thinks Job erred in, in his attempt to justify himself. He quoted the following three expressions from Job's words in his speeches.

33.7.3.en: Saying, I am clean without transgression.

33.8.0.en: I am innocent; neither is there iniquity in me [9].

33.8.1.en: The first error Elihu raised is Job's justifying himself. It is true that Job told God that he knows he is not wicked, and that he holds fast to righteousness, and other similar expressions, but at the same time he confessed that he is a sinner and that he would not be justified before God (Job 7:21; 9:29-30; 13:23, 26).

33.8.2.en: Elihu did not quote Job's words as they were, nor did Job's words carry a justification of himself, but rather a facing of the accusations against him, that he is a hypocrite and that he is wicked.

33.8.3.en: "I am innocent": the Hebrew word here is chap, derived from Chopap, and it means to cover, to protect, and also to wash or purify.

33.8.4.en: Behold, he findeth occasions against me.

33.9.0.en: He counteth me for his enemy [10].

33.9.1.en: Elihu accuses him of having said of God that He picks out faults against him, and watches for every opportunity against him as if he were an enemy. Perhaps he concluded this from Job's saying to God: "For now thou numberest my steps: dost thou not watch over my sin? My transgression is sealed up in a bag, and thou fabricatest against me beyond mine iniquity" (Job 14:16-17). "Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and holdest me for thine enemy?" (Job 13:24). "He hath also kindled his wrath against me, and he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies" (Job 19:11).

33.9.2.en: He putteth my feet in the stocks.

33.10.1.en: He took this accusation from Job's saying: "Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; and upon the roots of my feet thou hast dug" (Job 13:27).

33.10.2.en: Thus Job pictures God as one who is occupied with his sin, scrutinizing it and sealing it up, so that it may stand as a witness against him, and that He deals with him as an enemy, bearing wrath against him; He binds him in the stocks so that he may not escape the coming judgment and the divine verdict against him.

33.11.s.en: A. God has authority over man

33.11.0.en: 12 "Behold, in this thou art not just: I will answer thee, that God is greater than man. 13 Why dost thou strive against him? for he giveth not account of any of his matters.

33.11.1.en: Behold, in this thou art not just.

33.11.3.en: That God is greater than man [12].

33.11.4.en: To one who does not know that God is greater than man, this saying seems to need no recounting, but Elihu said it for a particular purpose. For he directed it to a man suffering grave successive calamities, without Job knowing what lay behind these calamities. What Elihu meant was that Job, the weak man, must submit to the divine chastisements, even if he does not grasp God's judgments concerning these chastisements. All that is fitting for him to know is that God is just, and that there is no injustice in Him, and that what befell Job is the fruit of his errors.

33.11.5.en: St. John Chrysostom holds that when Job cried out to God, saying: [He would not answer me] (Job 9:15), Elihu answered him: {Tell me, He whom you reproach for not inclining His ear to your entreaty, what is the proof that He does not hear you? He chastens and punishes! This is His rule for the reform of the condition of men}.

33.11.6.en: * The prophet David was compelled, under the weight of the blows, to utter exaggerated words, and then he returned to contemplate his origin, saying: [I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; for thou hast made me] (Ps 39:9). For he considered in what rank he was created, and learned the justice of the blow that had fallen on him.

33.11.8.en: * If we had no adversaries there would be no battle and no reward set apart for the victors, and the Kingdom of Heaven would not have been offered to us. "Our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" (2 Cor 4:17). And none of us would have hope of the great glory in the coming life as the result of patience in bearable afflictions.

33.11.9.en: * The temporary sorrow was no small matter for anyone, since they have perfect love for God in Christ Jesus, shed abroad in their hearts by the Holy Spirit.

33.11.10.en: Origen Why dost thou strive against him?

33.12.0.en: For he giveth not account of any of his matters [13].

33.12.1.en: Elihu reproaches Job because he enters into a quarrel with God; he questions Him and awaits a quick answer.

33.12.2.en: God loves man as His creature made in His image, and does what pleases (God), even if man does not grasp His divine plan. God does what is for man's edification, even if in many circumstances man does not grasp what lies behind the divine dealings.

33.12.3.en: It is fitting for man to trust in God's love and His surpassing fatherhood, wisdom and power, and so to receive everything from God's hand with joy and trust, as a child receives from his parents' hands what they do with him, until day by day he comes to understand the parents' plan for him.

33.12.4.en: Instead of entering into a quarrel with God, it is fitting for us to trust that He will not err, that He is a doer of good things, and that one day we shall mature spiritually and come to know His plan toward us.

33.12.5.en: Our part is submission and obedience with joy and trust in His wisdom, not entering into a quarrel with Him. For woe to him who strives with his Maker, a potsherd among the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or thy work, He hath no hands?" (Isa 45:9).

33.13.s.en: B. By the use of dreams and visions

33.13.0.en: 14 For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not. 15 In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed.

33.13.1.en: For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not [14].

33.13.2.en: Perhaps Elihu means that God spoke with Job when he was in prosperity and had many good things, and since he did not listen to God, He spoke with him in the language of successive afflictions, and yet Job did not grasp God's purposes and did not understand His words. So God sometimes speaks to us in the language of pain and affliction in order to purify us, so that we hear His voice and see Him revealed in our lives.

33.13.3.en: "Every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit" (Jn 15:2).

33.13.4.en: "God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God" (Ps 62:11).

33.13.5.en: He uses every means to speak with us: at times through the many good things He gives us, at times through His holy word, and sometimes through dreams and visions, and when we do not listen to Him, He speaks to us in the language of afflictions and sufferings, such as illnesses or troubles at work or material or moral losses, and so on.

33.13.6.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that it is natural for the suffering heart, when it sees matters going contrary to what it desires, to long to hear an answer from God as to why things go this way and not that. It longs to find an explanation for the events that pass over it. Elihu answers him that God does not answer man in a private, solitary talk with man's heart, but gives the answer through the Holy Scriptures once and not twice, that is, there is no need for God to give us the answer directly, as though repeating what He had already announced through the Holy Bible, but man has not noticed God's answer to him. It is fitting for us to grasp God's answer through His dealings with those who went before us, as examples for those who come after them, and not to expect Him to repeat the answer a second time (Job 33:14)..

33.13.7.en: He gives us an example of this: when an affliction comes upon us we find our consolation in what befell St. Paul, who suffered from weakness of the body, and heard the divine voice: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor 12:9). This was said to St. Paul when he suffered pain, so that it would not be said to each one individually, but that this saying be counted as offered beforehand to every sufferer.

33.13.8.en: The Father spoke once, when the divine Word was begotten eternally, and there is no other word that He begets that shares with Him the divine essence and is equal to Him in the same essence.

33.14.0.en: In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed [15].

33.14.1.en: By slumbering he means light sleep, in which a man is in a state between sleeping and waking.

33.14.2.en: Job had said earlier: "Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions" (Job 7:14). It was fitting for him to realize that God wished to give him a certain message through these frightening dreams and fearful visions. The Syriac version reads: "Not by lips does He teach, but by dreams and visions in the night."

33.14.3.en: When a man is in quietness, far from the confusions of life and the daily preoccupations, like one in a doze of sleep, he can listen to the divine voice amid the calm of his thoughts and inner emotions.

33.14.4.en: * What is meant by the word of God being made known to us in a dream, except that we do not learn the secret things of God while we are awake in worldly desires? In a dream the outer senses rest, and inner things can be discerned. So, if we wish to contemplate inner things, let us rest from outward occupations. Truly the voice of God is heard as in a dream when our minds are at rest, we rest from the noise of this world, and we reflect on the divine commandments in their depths, in the deep stillness of the mind.

33.14.5.en: So when the saints are obliged by the necessity of duties to busy themselves with outward things, they always return with longing to study the secrets of their hearts. Thus they ascend to the height of hidden thought, and learn as though from the Law on the mountain, when they put aside the disturbances of temporal affairs and meditate on the judgments of the divine will. So Moses himself often withdrew to the tabernacle of the congregation in doubtful matters, asking God secretly, and learning the decisions he had to make... So in the Song of Songs, the bride who says: "I sleep, but my heart waketh" (Song 5:2) heard the voice of the bridegroom in dreams...

33.14.6.en: And since all the saints, as long as they are in this life, see the secrets of the divine nature only through likenesses (for they have not yet acquired a clearer view of it, to see it as it is), therefore, after Elihu said that God speaks to us in a dream, he rightly added: "in a vision of the night." For the night is the present life, and as long as we are in it, we are covered with a light mist of uncertain imaginings, in so far as we are concerned with inner things. He added fittingly: [slumbering upon their beds]. For to the saints slumbering upon their beds is to rest in the chambers of the mind. So it is written: [Let the saints be joyful in glory: let them rejoice upon their beds] (Ps 149:5).

33.14.8.en: * The Lord commands (man) to leave his confused life and cleave to the One, to draw near to the grace of Him who offers eternal life.

33.14.9.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * Martha was concerned to feed the Lord, while Mary was concerned that the Lord should feed her. Through Martha the feast was prepared for the Lord, this feast in which Mary rejoiced.

33.14.10.en: * I say that in these two women the two lives were represented: the present life and the life to come; the life of striving and the life of rest; the life of sorrow and the life of blessedness; the temporal life and the eternal life...

33.14.11.en: What does this life bear? I am not speaking of a wicked, evil, malicious, luxurious, ungrateful life, but a life of striving filled with sufferings and fears, whose peace trials take away... And I say that the two lives are not harmful, indeed both are worthy of praise, but one is full of toil and the other is easy...

33.14.12.en: In Martha we find a picture of present things, and in Mary the things to come.

33.14.13.en: What Martha does we do now; what Mary does we hope to do. Let us do the first work well, so that we may receive the second in its fullness.

33.14.14.en: St. Augustine * The greatest good does not lie in works in themselves, however great their importance, but in contemplation of the Lord, who is truly "the one thing"... As for his saying, "shall not be taken away from her," he revealed that the other's portion can be taken away from her, because bodily services cannot remain with man eternally, whereas Mary's longing will have no end.

33.15.0.en: 16 Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction, 17 That he may withdraw man from his purpose, and hide pride from man. 18 He keepeth back his soul from the pit, and his life from perishing by the sword.

33.15.1.en: Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction [16].

33.15.2.en: In the calm of the soul, far from the confusions of life, God opens the ears of man to hear, with the prophet Samuel, the divine voice that Eli the priest did not hear. In the stillness of the night Samuel lifts up his heart, saying: [Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth].

33.15.3.en: God opens the ears of man to hear what those around him do not hear. God reveals to him some of His divine secrets, uncovers the truth to him, and shows him His divine will. "And sealeth their instruction," that is, He puts a seal on His warnings and chastisements to them, meaning that they are precious in God's eyes for their benefit; He treasures them for the edification of His children, so He seals them as one who confirms them.

33.15.4.en: In ancient times contracts were sealed so that they would be kept safe, with no hand stretched out to change them. So God regards chastisement as a covenant of love between God and His children, and seals it with His heavenly seal, as though He sealed a will He had given them to enjoy an inheritance or a share of it.

33.15.5.en: God seals their instruction, that is, He promises that behind it are many blessings that cannot be revoked. Behind afflictions are sealed divine promises that do not change.

33.15.6.en: * [Then he openeth the ears of men, and their teaching, and trains them by chastisement] [16]. There are four ways by which a man is strongly moved to practice remorse:

33.15.7.en: When he remembers his sins and sees where he is.

33.15.8.en: Or when he fears the judgments of God's judgment and examines himself, and so knows where he will be.

33.15.9.en: Or when he observes carefully the evils of the present life, and grieves over where he stands.

33.15.10.en: Or when he contemplates the blessings of his heavenly homeland, which he does not yet enjoy, and grieves that he has not yet reached it.

33.15.11.en: Paul remembered his sins and grieved over what he had been, for he said: "I am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God" (1 Cor 15:9).

33.15.12.en: Again, when he carefully weighed the divine judgment, he feared lest his position should be bad in this matter, for he says: "Lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" (1 Cor 9:27).

33.15.13.en: Again he contemplated the evils of the present life, for he said: "Whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord" (2 Cor 5:6). And: "I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members. O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" (Rom 7:23-24).

33.15.14.en: He also contemplated the blessings of his heavenly homeland, for he says: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known" (1 Cor 13:12), "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens" (2 Cor 5:1). Looking to the blessings of this house, he says to the Ephesians: "That ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of his mighty power" (Eph 1:18-19).

33.16.0.en: That he may withdraw man from his purpose, and hide pride from man [17].

33.16.1.en: Since man's nature has become corrupt, what occupies him is sin, and what dominates him is pride. So God allows chastisements and seals them in order to draw the believer away from his sin so that he may enjoy God's righteousness, and pride may be hidden from him lest it creep into his heart and mind, and he may live in a spirit of humility.

33.16.2.en: "Pride" is a dangerous pit into which even the religious often fall, like the Pharisees; therefore God covers the pit and fills it in, so that believers may not fall into it.

33.16.3.en: * What is man's own work, if not sin? It is rightly said, then, that when man is turned from what he does, he will be freed from pride. In disobeying the commandments of our Creator by sin, we exalt ourselves against Him. It is as though man throws off the yoke of God's authority whenever he disdains to submit to Him in obedience. On the other hand, he who wishes to avoid what he does calls to mind what he was made by God, and in humility returns to the order of his creation when he flies from his own works, and loves himself as God made him in the beginning.

33.17.0.en: He keepeth back his soul from the pit, and his life from perishing by the sword [18].

33.17.1.en: While the wicked spend every effort to achieve their evil goals and satisfy their pride, their souls fall into the pit of pride and perish in this present world and in the age to come. But God intervenes by every means, especially by allowing chastisements, to rescue them from this eternal death.

33.17.2.en: The word "soul" refers to the whole man, for death overtakes the body as well as the soul, the whole being of man.

33.17.3.en: The word "pit, shaachat" perhaps means a trap set by hunters for wild animals to fall into (Ps 7:15; 9:15), or a hollow filled with mire (Job 9:31), or a prison (Isa 51:14), or a tomb in the shape of a great cave (Job 17:13; Ps 30:9). It is clear that what is meant here is the grave, where man's life on earth ends.

33.17.4.en: * [Rescuing his soul from corruption, and his life from perishing by the sword] [18]. For every sinner, because of his corruption here by sin, is bound to pass over to the sword of punishment, so that he is justly punished in that world with the very sins in which he delighted in this world.

33.18.0.en: 19 He is chastened also with pain upon his bed, and the multitude of his bones with strong pain: 20 So that his life abhorreth bread, and his soul dainty meat. 21 His flesh is consumed away, that it cannot be seen; and his bones that were not seen stick out. 22 Yea, his soul draweth near unto the grave, and his life to the destroyers.

33.18.1.en: He is chastened also with pain upon his bed, and the multitude of his bones with strong pain [19].

33.18.2.en: God allows sufferings to befall some of His believers so that they are confined to bed, and in this He does not seek their pain, but to restrain their desire toward sin. In moments of affliction a man rethinks his life, and is given the opportunity to think about his eternal destiny.

33.18.3.en: Elihu makes clear here that affliction is a work of chastisement for edification, which God uses in a spirit of tender fatherhood, for the repentance of His children, their return to Him, and their enjoyment of fellowship in the glories.

33.18.4.en: The bed, the couch, or the resting place indicates either bodily pleasures, or rest in the practice of good works, or temporary rest. When the Lord Christ healed the paralytic He told him to take up his bed and walk (Mt 9:6), that is, no longer to sleep in the pleasures of the body, but by the word of the Lord to carry the bed of his sickness and be rid of his sins.

33.18.5.en: Here he declares that God chastens the man who has fallen into the pleasures of the body on his bed, so that the pleasures themselves become the source of his pain and chastisement. What he thinks the secret of his joy becomes for him the cause of his sorrow.

33.18.6.en: As for the bones that stick out, they indicate in Holy Scripture the virtues, for it is written: [The Lord keepeth all their bones: not one of them is broken] (Ps 34:20). They do not indicate here the bones of the body but the powers of the mind. For many bones of the martyrs were broken, in the bodily sense, as the legs of the thief to whom it was said: "Today shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Jn 19:32; Lk 23:43) were broken. For when He chastens us through our bodily desires, the boasting in our virtues is dispelled within us, and we confess our weakness. Through chastisement we realize our weakness, and without it we count ourselves strong in the life of virtue by our own abilities.

33.19.0.en: So that his life abhorreth bread, and his soul dainty meat [20].

33.19.1.en: Among the chastisements that God uses is the permitting of illness which makes a man lose his appetite even for eating bread, for his soul loathes it; and this is a profitable chastisement for sufferers, for they no longer find pleasure in delights and luxury.

33.19.2.en: A man loathes the sumptuous foods that he used to desire, and now finds repugnant.

33.19.3.en: The psalmist says of the foolish who are humbled by their iniquities: "Their soul abhorreth all manner of meat; and they draw near unto the gates of death" (Ps 107:18). And the wise man describes the state of the dead: "And desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets" (Eccl 12:5).

33.19.4.en: After speaking of the power of divine chastisement, which lifts man from the bed of bodily pleasures and dispels his boasting in a virtuous life as though it were the work of his own hands, he says here that He makes his bread defiled in his lips, so that his life abhors bread, and his soul loathes dainty meat. What does he mean by bread and dainty meat but the pleasures in which he found a special delight that he could not do without? Through chastisement his bread turns for him into a loathsome defilement, as he realizes the vanity of bodily pleasures, and the sweetness of the dainty food turns into a bitterness he cannot bear.

33.20.0.en: His flesh is consumed away, that it cannot be seen; and his bones that were not seen stick out [21].

33.20.1.en: The body that man prized and took pride in for its beauty and strength is consumed as though it had vanished, and becomes as though it did not exist, and the bones which were hidden, clothed with flesh, stand out from extreme thinness and illness, as though they had become bare.

33.20.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on this phrase, which in his writings is translated: "His flesh is consumed, and his bones that were covered are laid bare," that the flesh here indicates the desires of the flesh, and the bones the virtues of the soul. For through the rod of chastisement the desires of the flesh are consumed and have no authority over us, and the virtues that were hidden are uncovered, and shine forth amid the divine chastisement.

33.20.3.en: * No one learns how far he has progressed except in affliction, because in prosperity desires cannot be distinguished from spiritual strength. When the Apostles were chastised they were commanded not to speak any more in the name of Jesus. But they rejoiced greatly that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for the name of Jesus. And with confidence they answered their adversaries saying: [We ought to obey God rather than men] (see Acts 5:29). Behold, you see the power of faith shine more vividly in the midst of affliction. Behold, you see the soundness of (the desires of) the flesh cut off, and the bones of their virtues laid bare. It was said of them by Wisdom: [God proved them, and found them worthy for himself] (Wis 3:5). For when they are tested by the blasts of the adversary they are found worthy by the baring of their bones. For the strength of every man is known only in affliction.

33.21.0.en: Yea, his soul draweth near unto the grave, and his life to the destroyers [22].

33.21.1.en: Here he means that the man who has fallen into affliction becomes like one suffering severe pains that almost end his life, and he is led to the destroyers, that is, the angels of death, the angels appointed by God to take men's spirits.

33.21.2.en: * [His soul draweth near unto corruption, and his life to the destroyers] [22]. To the extent that he is led by affliction and realizes that his strength is drawing near to death, he works to find a solution, finds the true foundation of life, by flying to the protection that comes from trust in God.

33.22.0.en: If there be a messenger with him, a mediator, one among a thousand, to shew unto man his uprightness [23].

33.22.1.en: Opinions differ in the interpretation of this phrase. It reads in the Septuagint: "If there be a thousand angels of death, not one of them can wound him mortally. If he is determined in his heart to return to the Lord, when his accusation against him appears to man and his folly is shown, He will help him so that he does not fall into death, and will renew his flesh like smooth plaster on a wall, and will fill his bones with marrow, and make his body tender like a child's." The Vulgate translation reads: "If there be an angel speaking for him, one of a thousand, to declare man's righteousness, it will weigh upon him and he will say: Deliver him who falls into corruption; I have found this one for whom I am suitable." And in the Chaldean version: "If there be found merit in him, an angel is prepared, a comforter, one among a thousand accusers, to declare to man his uprightness; I have found a ransom." 1. The first opinion: that this angel is a man. Munster and Isidore hold that he is an excellent teacher sent to the sick to teach the will of God. Junius and Termillius hold that he is a prophet. Codurcus holds that he refers here to the case of Abimelech, who was struck with sickness because of Sarah, and that the angel is a prophet sent to declare to him that God is righteous (Gen 20). Umbreit holds that the angel here is Elihu himself, whom God sent to Job to declare the truth concerning the divine dispensation and the mystery of allowing sorrows to befall men. Others hold that the speech here concerns the faithful servant of God who visits the sick and the suffering and declares to them God's plan, without naming a particular person. 2. The second opinion: that the speech concerns God's sending His angels to declare His will to men, especially to sufferers, and to assure them that God wants to show them His mercy if they return to Him in repentance. St. Jerome, for example, holds that the speech here refers to an angel standing in God's presence, whose work is to guide mankind and set its affairs right. 3. The third opinion: that the speech here is a prophecy about the person of the Lord Christ, and among those who proclaimed this opinion is St. Augustine.

33.22.2.en: * Who is this messenger (angel), but he whom the prophet called: "the Angel of Counsel, the Mighty"?

33.22.3.en: * Our Physician from above, since He found us under the weight of many diseases like this... came to us as man, but as righteous to those who are in sin. He agreed with us in the truth of His nature (His humanity), and differed from us in the power of His righteousness.

33.22.4.en: A sinful man cannot be set right except by God. But it was necessary that He (Christ) who accomplishes his healing should be visible and perceived by the senses, in order that He might set right our former evil life by setting before us a pattern to imitate. It was not possible for God to be seen by man. Therefore He became man in order to be seen. The holy, invisible God appeared as a visible man like us, so that, appearing as one like us, He might teach us by His holiness and put an end to our sickness by the power of His skill...

33.22.5.en: Since there was in Him no admixture of sin, He was not subject to any punishment as a matter of necessity. He subdued our transgression by overcoming it. He submitted to our punishment because of His compassion for us, and as He Himself says: [I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again] (see Jn 10:18). Again, He did not rise like other men, for our resurrection will be accomplished at the end of the world, but His resurrection was celebrated on the third day. We indeed rise by Him, but He rises by Himself.

33.23.0.en: Then he is gracious unto him, and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom [24].

33.23.1.en: As Elihu refers to the Mediator, our Lord Jesus Christ, he speaks of His role in the salvation of man and his enjoyment of redemption, rescuing him from descending into the abyss of the kingdom of darkness, and giving him eternal life instead of eternal destruction.

33.23.2.en: * He will be gracious to him, and say: [Deliver him from going down to corruption: I have found a way to his ransom] [24]. The Mediator between God and man, the man Christ Jesus, since He took the form of a man. In His compassion His Father says on behalf of the man who is saved: [Deliver him from going down to corruption].

33.23.3.en: We are set free by the righteousness of the Almighty Savior, as He Himself says: "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed" (Jn 8:36). It is well said on behalf of this redeemed man: [His soul draweth near unto corruption] (see Job 33:22), and now he declares that he does not go down to corruption. It is as though he says: Since he realizes, through the sense of his weakness, that he is not far from corruption, therefore may he not go down to the death of corruption, for he truly goes down to corruption if he counts himself by his own strength to have gone far from it. But since he draws near in humility, he must be received with mercy. For as he confessed his weakness by nature, he is strengthened against the sins that wrestle with him. For he who boasts of himself beyond what he is goes down by the weight of his pride, and sinks to greater depths...
